entries.title: Kinematics and End Effector
entries.summary: This section covers the signal and control flow for the single-rail 3-PRRR parallel manipulator and its sample gripper.
entries.body:
# Kinematics and End Effector

**Time.** 00:00–00:00, location.

## Discussion

This section covers the signal and control flow for the single-rail 3-PRRR parallel manipulator and its sample gripper.

### 1. Overall System Pipeline

From a target coordinate to the realized end-effector position.

| Step | Stage | What happens |
|------|-------|--------------|
| 1 | **Spatial Target Input** | Desired end-effector location, target (X, Y, Z) |
| 2 | **Kinematic Solver** (Raspberry Pi / host) | Closed-form 3-PRRR inverse kinematics: (X, Y, Z) → (d1, d2, d3) |
| 3 | **Motion Controller** (32-bit MCU firmware) | Displacement to steps via `STEPS_PER_MM`; pulse generation and trapezoidal velocity ramping |
| 4 | **Actuation & Drive Train** | 3x stepper motors with TMC2209 silent drivers; continuous GT2 timing belt loop |
| 5 | **Single-Rail Transmission** (3-PRRR) | 3x collinear carriages on a central extrusion track; passive linkage arms with free revolute joints |
| 6 | **End-Effector Output** | Realized 3D coordinate (X, Y, Z); electromechanical parallel-jaw sample gripper |

### 2. Gripper Operation Sequence

Full lifecycle of a pick, transit and release.

1. **Pre-grip and object detection**
   - ToF IR sensor (VL53L1X) checks that the vial is present.
   - The Pi commands the lead-screw motor to start closing.
2. **Active clamping**
   - A micro stepper drives the parallel jaws inward.
   - The strain gauge load cell flexes under contact force.
3. **Strain gauge signal conditioning**
   - The Wheatstone bridge outputs a differential mV signal.
   - The HX711 24-bit ADC amplifies and digitizes it at 80 Hz.
4. **Force comparison: is F_meas ≥ F_target?**
   - **No:** continue driving the motor inward and return to step 3.
   - **Yes:** halt the motor immediately and engage holding torque.
5. **In-transit sample drop protection**
   - Rail transit begins along the Y-axis track.
   - The strain gauge is polled continuously in the background.
   - If F_meas drops below the threshold, trigger a drop alert.
6. **Sample release**
   - Target destination reached.
   - The lead-screw motor reverses to retract the jaws.

### 3. Gripper Force Control Loop

The closed loop that clamps the sample at a fixed force and monitors for drops.

1. **Initial grip command**
   - Set the target force threshold (e.g., F_target = 2.0 N).
   - The Pi commands the lead-screw stepper to close the jaws.
2. **Continuous signal sampling**
   - The lead screw closes the parallel jaws on the sample.
   - The HX711 samples the load cell at 80 Hz.
3. **Threshold check: is F_meas ≥ F_target?**
   - **No:** continue the motor inward drive and return to step 2.
   - **Yes:** halt the motor instantly and engage holding current.
4. **In-transit sample drop monitor**
   - The rail moves the sample along the Y-axis track.
   - Background check: if F_meas falls below 0.2 N, alert and halt.

### 4. Z-Height Closed-Loop Correction

Uses the ToF sensor to correct vertical error against the benchtop.

1. **Real-time distance read:** the VL53L1X measures height above the benchtop (Z_measured).
2. **Error calculation:** ΔZ = Z_target − Z_measured.
3. **Tolerance check: does the magnitude of ΔZ exceed 0.2 mm?**
   - **No:** maintain the current trajectory; no adjustment needed.
   - **Yes:** recalculate the 3-PRRR IK and adjust the d1, d2, d3 carriages.

### 5. Motion Planning and StallGuard Safety

From target coordinate to motion, with jam detection.

1. **Spatial coordinate target:** input the desired (X, Y, Z) in mm.
2. **Closed-form kinematic solver:** the Raspberry Pi computes carriage positions (d1, d2, d3) using linear 3-PRRR algebraic equations [4].
3. **Pulse generation and motion**
   - The motion controller converts (d1, d2, d3) to step counts.
   - The TMC2209 drivers execute a trapezoidal velocity profile.
4. **StallGuard safety back-EMF loop**
   - The TMC2209 continuously monitors motor back-EMF.
   - **No spike:** continue motion.
   - **Spike:** a physical obstacle or jam is detected, so trigger an emergency interrupt and disable motor torque.

## Decisions

- **Main controller:** [Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (4 GB)](https://www.pishop.ca/product/raspberry-pi-4-model-b-4gb/)
- **Low-level communication:** STM32 Nucleo connected to the stepper drivers

## Action items

- [ ] Kinematic Solver to target step counts — Khushmeet, 2026-11-07

entries.title: SHARE — PDP
entries.body:
# Idea finalization and PDP preparation

## Discussion

### Needs assessment

- Completed a needs assessment for the concept.
- Identified the need for better equipment utilization in self-driving laboratories.
- Drafted the problem statement, objectives, criteria, and constraints.

### Solution concepts

- Outlined our proposal for a bench-mounted sample-handling system.
- Developed several distinct solution morphologies.

### Concept selection

- Defined the design criteria and assigned each a weight.
- Used the weights to build a decision matrix and scored each design in it.
- The monorail tripteron scored highest.

### Timeline

- Set a development timeline.

## Decisions

- The monorail tripteron is our selected design, because it scored highest in the weighted decision matrix.

entries.title: Monorail Tripteron
entries.body:
# Idea name Monorail Tripteron

## Problem
3D Printers are limited in printing long parts such as car pieces. 

## Proposed solution
Create a monorail tripteron system that spans a long y axis.

## Decision notes
N/A

## Objective
- Print parts longer than a desktop printer
- Accuracy on the y-axis
- Affordable
- Easy to calibrate/set up
- Device should be able to fit on a workbench

## Constraints
- Device must use a linear rail
- Device must run on wall power
- Device must not deflect over 1mm
- Device must have an e-stop

## Criteria
- Volume/dimensions
- Accuracy
- Print speed
- Calibration time
- Cost

entries.title: AR Snowboard Goggles
entries.body:
# Idea name AR Snowboard Goggles

## Problem
Snowboarders and skiiers use apps such as Slopes and Strava to track their stats on runs and to locate their friends on other parts of the mountain. However using your phone for these apps poses several problems while on the mountain:
1. drains phone battery quickly
2. unable to check speed while on run
3. need to take off gloves and check phone to use apps

## Proposed solution
Create a goggle attachment that creates a display of speeds and location arrows. The locational arrows point to people in your party and/or mountain structures (chalet, lifts).

## Decision notes
N/A

## Objective
- Display current speed, heading, altitude and direction to nearest friend
- The attachment should be less than $250
- light weight < 500g
- Device should record video footage
- Device should non-invasively attaches to most helmet/goggles
- Device should be water resistant

## Constraints
- Device must operate in sub-zero temperatures
- Device must meet IP44 for snow/water resistance
- Device must not require permanent modifications of goggles or helmet
- Battery must last at least 4 hours
- The refresh rate must be at least 1Hz 
- Device must be usable with winter gloves

## Criteria
- Mass
- Volume/dimensions
- Water/particle resistance
- Battery life
- Refresh rate
- Cost
- Operating temperature

entries.title: Multispectral Search and Rescue Snow Goggles
entries.body:
# Multispectral Search and Rescue Snow Goggles

## Problem
Search and resuce (SAR) workers in harsh environments (i.e. blizzards, snow storms, avalanches) have limited visibility when responding to SOS reports. 

## Proposed solution
Develop a pair of multispectral (i.e. IR, Thermal) goggles which can automatically determine which specturm gives the greatest visibility/contrast. Additionally, goggles can also have HUD which displays location to nearest search party member to assist in search efforts. 

## Why it's worth doing
Since SAR workers will already be wearing snow goggles in extreme environments, a multispectral pair of goggles could enhance successful SAR efforts by giving SAR workers enhanced visibility, especially post-avalanche or during heavy snowstorms for example. 

## Concerns and risks
- Overall package would be too bulky/heavy to be practical
- Refresh rate might not be fast enough and may cause dizzines or motion sickness
- Battery life must last long enough to be useful
- Display resolution must be high enough to allow for small/far away targets to be discernable from wildlife

## Objectives
- Weight should be less 500g
- Battery life should be at least 8 hours 
- Spectral band switching should occur automatically during contrast change
- Refresh rate should be at least 72Hz to mitigate nausea
- Should be able to identify a person within a 3 metre range
- The device should be able to work in cold climates

## Constraints
- Device must operate in sub-zero temperatures
- Device must meet IP44 for snow/water resistance
- Device must not extend further than 10cm beyond a regular goggle profile
- Battery must last 6 hours with continuous use
- The refresh rate must be at least 60Hz 
- Device must be usable with winter gloves

## Criteria
- Mass
- Volume/dimensions
- Water/particle resistance
- Battery life
- Refresh rate
- Visible range
- Cost
- Operating temperature
- Spectral switching time
- Resolution

## Decision Notes
- N/A
